label: provisional
paradigm: These criteria serve a buyer choosing what to purchase, new or pre-owned: an evidence-based, value-aware buyer who wants an informed view of history and context. They are one reasonable buyer's stance, not the only one, and this version is provisional: drafted from published sources, not yet compiled or ratified.

change_log.reason: Drafted from Time+Tide on lifetime servicing costs, WatchTime on movement serviceability, a European Watch Company buyer's guide (a retailer), and the Teddy content audit of 2026-11-14, whose 'mistakes' video supplies most of the practitioner rules.

spec_fields.band: lower-case string describing the strap or bracelet, for example "black alligator leather strap"

wearer.statement: Budget for ownership, not just purchase: servicing over the years owned, insurance, storage, straps and import duties.
Whether the buyer is buying new or pre-owned changes what to check: a pre-owned bargain can carry a service bill that erases the discount, and service records have to be read, not counted.

watch.statement: What the money buys: finishing, engineering and specifications per unit of price, judged against peers in the same price band. Claims of 'diminishing returns' at the top are asserted, not measured.
Expected service interval and price for the movement over the years the buyer will own it; entry-level movements may cost several times their price in servicing over a lifetime.
Widely used movements with parts in ready supply can be serviced cheaply and locally; in-house movements tend to cost more and go back to the brand.
An existing market where the watch is traded, so it can be sold if tastes change. Buying for appreciation is fragile; buy a good watch and treat held value as a bonus.
For pre-owned: pay a box-and-papers premium only on references whose resale market rewards it; one retailer puts the premium at 13 to 23 percent of resale value, unsourced.
For pre-owned: read what the service records say (what was done, by whom, which parts replaced), not just whether they exist; originality of dial, hands and parts matters.
Buy the version with the bracelet if the buyer might want one: a luxury bracelet bought later can cost four figures, and a bracelet may retain value better at resale.
